draft.title: Evocative vocabulary
card: Evocative words call up strong pictures and feelings in the reader. They are chosen for more than their basic meaning.
Compare "The boy walked home" with "The boy trudged home." Trudged suggests heavy, tired steps, so the reader pictures and feels the tiredness.
Evocative words often carry the writer's judgement quietly. Calling a crowd a "mob" rather than a "group" makes it seem unruly and a little frightening.
To spot them, ask what a word suggests beyond its plain meaning, and what feeling it creates.
draft.remember: Evocative words add picture, feeling and a quiet judgement.

a.q: In which sentence is the word choice most evocative?
opts: The dog slunk under the table
The dog went under the table
The dog moved under the table
The dog was under the table
a.why: Slunk suggests a guilty, sneaking movement, so it creates a picture and a feeling. Went, moved and was only give the plain action or position.
a.clue: Which verb makes you picture how the dog moved?

b.q: A writer describes a shop as a "cramped, gloomy hole" instead of a "small, dim shop". What effect do the evocative words have?
opts: They make the reader see the shop negatively
They make the reader think the shop is cosy
They give the reader plain facts about size
They show the writer has no opinion
b.why: Cramped, gloomy and hole carry unpleasant feelings, so they lead the reader to a negative view. Small and dim are more neutral, so the writer's judgement would be less clear.
b.clue: What feeling do cramped and gloomy bring?

a.best: The dog slunk under the table

b.best: They make the reader see the shop negatively

problems.detail: The card says evocative words 'often' carry the writer's judgement, but the remember line drops the qualifier. It says they add 'a quiet judgement' as if every evocative word does. Consider 'can add a quiet judgement'.
